edits.html: Neurofibromatosis type 1: tumor risk Optic nerve glioma — the most common brain tumor in neurofibromatosis type 1; usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma of one or both optic nerves or the chiasm · Presentation — insidious vision loss, proptosis and optic atrophy · Eye surveillance — children with neurofibromatosis type 1 need an eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18 · Pheochromocytoma — risk also raised · No established link — medulloblastoma, craniopharyngioma, and arteriovenous malformation, which belongs to Wyburn-Mason syndrome
edits.note: NBME Q12: optic nerve glioma is the NF1 tumor risk; distractor lesions without a link

edits.html: · How NBME framed it: a well 17-year-old at a sports physical has about 10 light brown macules and axillary freckling, and the syndrome is never named. After puberty only macules over 15 mm count, so the axillary freckling supplies the second criterion. The lead-in asks which lesion carries a raised risk compared with the general population.

edits.html:
Salient decoyMedulloblastoma, for the teenager with 10 café-au-lait macules — The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia, but neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotCraniopharyngioma — A Rathke pouch remnant that causes bitemporal field loss; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotArteriovenous malformation — Retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations belong to Wyburn-Mason syndrome, not neurofibromatosis type 1
True-fact-wrong-slotCerebral aneurysm — An adult cause of intracranial hemorrhage; the tumor this skin pattern predicts is an optic nerve glioma
